units: two adjoining plots are set side by side by the person who manages the fruit trees
one of the plots is sheltered by a living hedge and a bank of earth
the other plot is open and exposed to the wind
the sheltered plot holds water for longer after rain
the open plot dries out quickly once the sun returns
the neighbour complains that the living hedge shades the young plants
the neighbour also complains that it harbours small mammals
the manager judges these drawbacks minor next to the water saved
helpful insects shelter in the low growth on the bank
both speakers reckon that harvests must be recorded over several cycles
text: The woman who looks after the orchard says she weighed up two neighbouring plots before deciding. A thick hedge runs along the edge of one, and a low bank of earth slows the water as it drains away. The other lies bare, with the wind sweeping across it right up to the fence. Damp lingers in the sheltered plot long after a shower, she says, while the open ground dries the moment the sun comes back. Her neighbour sees it differently. The hedge, he argues, steals light from the young shoots and gives cover to rats and mice. She has weighed that up too, and it counts for little beside the water she keeps. Helpful insects nest in the scrub along the bank, besides, and drift down to the blossom. On one thing the two of them agree: none of it proves anything unless each keeps a record of the crop, season after season.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the considered use of trees is not a recent practice
past generations picked out many uses for a single tree
the shoots springing from a stump cut to the ground served as fuel
the covering of the trunk was stripped as the sap began to rise again
this covering was used to prepare animal skins
leaves gathered at the end of the cycle fed the herds when grazing ran short
the woven living hedge served as a barrier and gave fruit
ditches at the foot of the earth banks dried the fields and held a store of water
this landscape was in truth a set of tools and not mere scenery
text: Think the careful use of trees is a recent idea? Not a bit of it. Our forebears had already sorted out what each one was good for, and their reckoning was finer than we tend to assume. Firewood came first, cut from the shoots that spring back out of a stump felled right down to the ground. Then came the bark, stripped off as the sap began to rise, and put to use for curing skins. Leaves were gathered late on and fed to the herds when the grazing ran thin. Add the living hedge, woven in place, which kept the stock in and gave berries into the bargain. And do not forget the ditches dug at the foot of the banks: they took the wet off the fields and held a store of water against a dry spell. Nothing at all was left lying about. What we take for scenery was in truth a whole set of tools.

units: the process begins on a plot left untended
in the first cycle tall grasses take charge of the ground
in the next cycle thorny plants move in
these thorny plants keep young shoots safe from animals that graze
the first trees to arrive spread by seed carried on the wind
these first trees grow fast but cope badly with a lack of light
slower species then come on beneath their cover
the edge of the wood shows the stages of the change at a glance
a fire, a violent gale or felling sends the plot back to the beginning
text: It starts with a patch of rough ground: land nobody mows any more, land that the eye reads as empty. Through the first season the tall grasses take charge and close the surface over. In the second, brambles and scrub move in, and behind the thorns the young shoots are safe from anything that grazes. Then come the pioneer trees, light things with flying seed, quick off the mark but poor at coping with shade. Underneath them slower species germinate, ready to wait many seasons before they push through the canopy. At the edge of the wood the sequence can be read in one look: low bushes in front, tall timber behind. Foresters call this a succession, and they point out that it has no fixed end. Fire, a gale or the saw sends it back to the beginning, and the whole order repeats itself.

units: the bank built to hold the water back gave way during the night
the keeper of the water works was asleep only a few paces off
he heard a dull sound followed by the bank sliding into the flow
an earlier clearing of the channel had torn out the roots that bound the edge
without those roots the silt was carried off at every rise of the water
the flood spread over the low fields and buried the crops under mud
the people living nearby blamed the rain at first
the keeper blamed the loss of the plants along the edge
shrubs with creeping roots were put back in the season that followed
the new planting now stands up to the current and holds the bank
text: On the night the embankment gave way, the man who kept the lock was asleep a few paces from the breach. He remembers a dull sound, then the slow slide of the bank into the current. What lay behind it came out later. The roots that had bound the edge together were torn out the autumn before, when the channel was dredged without much thought. With that framework gone the silt had nothing to grip, and every rise of the water took its share. The flood spread across the low meadows, drowning the fences and laying a skin of mud over the crops. The people along the water blamed the rain at first. The keeper pointed instead at the bare stumps in a row by the edge, saying the works had lost their living bones. Shrubs with creeping roots went in the season after. Now the young stems bend without breaking, and the bank holds.

units: an earth bank that crumbles in the rain ends up blocking the ditch below
the first step is to work out where the water comes in and where it sits
without that survey the planting will be washed out
the loose rubbish must be cleared and the dead stems cut off flush with the ground
the base of the trunk is left in place because its roots still bind the soil
short level shelves are cut in a staggered pattern to break the slope
shrubs with dense roots are set in and the ground is covered with shredded branches
watering is kept to the first cycle so that the roots go down for water
after two cycles scrub covers the face and the run-off no longer gathers
text: A bank that crumbles at every downpour will end up choking the ditch below it. Here is how to hold it in place for good. Work out first where the water comes in and where it sits; skip that survey and whatever you plant will be washed out. Clear the loose rubbish next, then cut the dead stems off flush with the ground, leaving the stools where they are, since their roots still bind the soil. Cut short level shelves into the face, offset from one row to the next, so that the slope is broken up. Set shrubs with dense roots along the back of each shelf, then mulch with branches shredded on the spot. Water through the first season only, or the roots will stay lazy near the surface. Check the take after heavy rain and replace anything that has dried out. Two seasons on, scrub covers the face and the run-off spreads.

units: two towns on the same watercourse settled on different answers
the floods of the previous year prompted these decisions
the first town raised its embankment and faced the foot of the bank with stone
the second bought low-lying farmland to take the overflow
pools were dug across the land that had been bought
the figures show a more evenly spread flow leaving the second town
the water held underground recovers further in the second town
leaders of the first town cite the shelter of a densely built quarter
the specialists hold that the two methods complete one another
text: Two towns on the same river settled on opposite answers after the floods of last season. The first had its embankment raised and the foot of the bank faced with stone, on the argument that protection ought to be plain to see and quick to build. The second chose instead to buy up low-lying farmland, dig pools across it and let the river spread there when it rises. Figures put before a public meeting show a clear gap. Flow leaving the second town is more evenly spread, and the water held underground there recovers further. Councillors from the first town reply that their scheme shelters a densely built quarter, which the other approach would not have covered. The engineers brought in conclude that the two answers complete one another rather than compete, and they advise using both along the valley.

units: a waterlogged patch lies below the path and is crossed on planks
the ground gives underfoot and brown water works up between the plants
three habitats follow one after another with no line drawn between them
a belt of tall hollow stems edges the entrance and shuts off the view
a thicket of low shrubs holds the middle ground
still water lingers under that thicket
a sheet of open water takes up the centre
birds, frogs and a crowd of insects use the place
the plants hold back particles and dissolved matter before they reach the ground water
text: Below the path the ground opens into a wetland, crossed on a run of planks. Underfoot it gives like a sponge, and brown water works its way up between the tussocks. Three habitats follow one after another with no line drawn between them. At the near edge a belt of tall hollow stems shuts off the view and rustles at the faintest breath of air. Beyond it lies a thicket of low shrubs, the bark smooth and supple, with dark pools of standing water held underneath. In the middle a sheet of open water takes in the sky, ringed by a soft margin that sinks under the boot. Nesting birds work the cover, frogs call from the shallows, and insects swarm over the lot. The plants act as a sieve as well, holding back particles and dissolved matter before they reach the ground water. Nothing here looks dramatic; few places nearby hold as much life.

units: the writer had no faith at first in a scrap of waste ground behind the flats
a building scheme meant to clear the growth and cover the plot
the scheme stopped when the money ran out
brambles had taken the whole plot two cycles on
the neighbours grumbled about it
a group from the street put forward cutting paths and mowing only the middle
the idea was laughed at to begin with
the birds came back and the children made the place their own
the council in the end had the plot listed as a natural space
the writer now stands up for this rough ground rather than a park laid out with a ruler
text: I had no faith in it at all, that scrap of waste ground wedged behind the flats. To begin with we were told a developer would clear the lot and cover it in concrete. Then the work stopped, the money having run out, and the plot was left exactly as it stood. Two seasons on, brambles had taken the whole thing and the neighbours were grumbling. A group from the street put forward an idea: cut a few paths through, keep the scrub along the sides and mow nothing but the middle. People laughed. Then the birds came back, the children got into the habit of tearing about in there, and the council had the plot listed at last as a natural space. My own view shifted somewhere along the way. I wanted a park laid out with a ruler; now I stand up for this useful mess. It costs next to nothing to keep and gives back more than a shaved lawn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a long spell without rain settled the trade of this raiser of young trees
she had been growing cereals until then
her yields fell away two cycles running
she turned her driest fields over to raising trees
she had to learn to tell trees apart and judge the health of a sapling
her first orders came from her neighbours
the people who look after rivers then ordered stock from her to hold banks together
her plants take hold better elsewhere because they came up on thin soil
she now has staff on the payroll and takes in trainees
from her old trade she kept the habit of writing everything down
text: A long drought settled the trade of the woman who now raises young trees at the edge of the village. She was running a cereal farm at the time, and watched her yields fall away two seasons running. With nothing worth cutting, she turned her driest fields over to a nursery of native trees. The switch forced a second craft on her: reading bark, judging the vigour of a sapling by the colour of its sap, sowing at the right moment. Orders came from her neighbours first, then from the people who look after rivers and wanted stock that would hold a bank together. Because her plants come up on thin soil, they take hold better once they are moved elsewhere. She has three on the payroll now and trains youngsters who travel a fair way to reach her. One habit survives from the old days: she writes everything down, season by season.

units: the quiet of the machinery is the first thing this reworked valley leaves you with
the place had once been tidied to excess
the bed of the stream had been pulled straight and its banks laid in masonry
the meadows had been drained by a network of ditches
the wild things had left the place
those who carried out the repair gave the stream its bends back
whole trunks were dropped into the bed on purpose
the wood edge was allowed to creep out over the meadows
walkers struggle to find a dry way through
the tree cover keeps the air cool and the current is slowed before the town
text: What strikes you first in this valley given back to the water is that no machine is running. The place had once been tidied to excess: the stream pulled straight, the banks laid in masonry, the meadows drained down to the last ditch. The result was a corridor rather than a landscape, and the wild things had gone. Whoever carried out the repair went the other way entirely. They gave the stream its bends again, dropped whole trunks into the bed and let the wood edge creep out over the grass. You could accuse them of indulging disorder, and walkers do struggle to find a dry way through. Even so, it convinces. Under the canopy that has grown back the air stays cool, dead wood feeds the insects, and the current sheds its load before it reaches the town. A quiet success, measured less by what it built than by what it let happen.
